claim: Patient H.M. was the first reported case of hippocampal amnesia.
source: Ever since the first report of the famous patient H.M. (Scoville and Milner, 1957), hippocampal (HPC) amnesia has played a fundamental role in the neuroscience of human memory (MacPherson and Della Sala, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scoville and Milner, 1957, which is the original report of patient H.M.

claim: Hippocampal amnesia has played a fundamental role in the neuroscience of human memory.
source: Ever since the first report of the famous patient H.M. (Scoville and Milner, 1957), hippocampal (HPC) amnesia has played a fundamental role in the neuroscience of human memory (MacPherson and Della Sala, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to MacPherson and Della Sala, 2019.

claim: Studies of amnesic patients have often produced inconsistent results.
source: Studies of amnesic patients have, however, often produced inconsistent results.
evidence: This is a general statement about the literature on amnesia, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Studies of amnesic patients have been criticized for attributing behavioral deficits solely to the hippocampus.
source: Such studies have been criticized for attributing behavioral deficits solely to the HPC (Squire and Wixted, 2011), despite the fact that focal damage may trigger more subtle structural and functional abnormalities across an extended HPC system, involving the thalamus and cingulate cortex (Aggleton, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Squire and Wixted, 2011.

claim: Focal hippocampal damage may trigger structural and functional abnormalities across an extended hippocampal system involving the thalamus and cingulate cortex.
source: Such studies have been criticized for attributing behavioral deficits solely to the HPC (Squire and Wixted, 2011), despite the fact that focal damage may trigger more subtle structural and functional abnormalities across an extended HPC system, involving the thalamus and cingulate cortex (Aggleton, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aggleton, 2014.

claim: Broader network abnormalities are well documented in focal conditions such as ischemic stroke.
source: Indeed, broader network abnormalities are well documented in other 'focal' conditions [e.g. ischemic stroke (Carter et al., 2010; Veldsman et al., 2018)] and have been demonstrated in small case series of amnesic patients (Hayes et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carter et al., 2010 and Veldsman et al., 2018.

claim: Broader network abnormalities have been demonstrated in small case series of amnesic patients.
source: Indeed, broader network abnormalities are well documented in other 'focal' conditions [e.g. ischemic stroke (Carter et al., 2010; Veldsman et al., 2018)] and have been demonstrated in small case series of amnesic patients (Hayes et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hayes et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013.

claim: Network abnormalities may be important in understanding memory impairment in neurological disease.
source: These abnormalities may be important in understanding memory impairment in neurological disease (Addis et al., 2007) but their explanatory potential is under-explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Addis et al., 2007.

claim: The explanatory potential of network abnormalities in memory impairment is under-explored.
source: These abnormalities may be important in understanding memory impairment in neurological disease (Addis et al., 2007) but their explanatory potential is under-explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research in the field.

claim: Some authors hold that recall relies on hippocampus-dependent recollection processes, whereas recognition additionally draws on familiarity mediated by non-hippocampal structures within the medial temporal lobe.
source: Some authors hold that recall relies on HPC-dependent recollection processes, whereas recognition additionally draws on familiarity, which is mediated by non-HPC structures within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) (Brown and Aggleton, 2001; Kafkas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown and Aggleton, 2001 and Kafkas et al., 2016.

claim: Some authors argue that recollection and familiarity do not dissociate within the medial temporal lobe.
source: Others argue that recollection and familiarity do not dissociate within the MTL (Wixted and Squire, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wixted and Squire, 2010.

claim: Some theorists posit that hippocampal processing is material-specific, with the hippocampus holding a privileged role in processing scenes or spatial stimuli.
source: Related to the above, some theorists posit that HPC processing is material-specific, whereby the HPC holds a privileged role in processing scenes or spatial stimuli and this function underpins its involvement in episodic memory and navigation (Maguire and Mullally, 2013; Graham et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maguire and Mullally, 2013 and Graham et al., 2010.

claim: An opposing view holds that the primary role of the hippocampus is the material-independent maintenance of information over a limited time period.
source: An opposing view holds that the primary role of the HPC is the material-independent maintenance of information over a limited time period (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Some reports have provided evidence for abnormal forgetting after medial temporal lobe damage.
source: Whereas some reports have provided evidence for abnormal forgetting after MTL damage (Huppert and Piercy, 1979; Isaac and Mayes, 1999), other studies have reported normal forgetting rates (Freed et al., 1987; Kopelman, 1985; McKee and Squire, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huppert and Piercy, 1979 and Isaac and Mayes, 1999.

claim: Other studies have reported normal forgetting rates after medial temporal lobe damage.
source: Whereas some reports have provided evidence for abnormal forgetting after MTL damage (Huppert and Piercy, 1979; Isaac and Mayes, 1999), other studies have reported normal forgetting rates (Freed et al., 1987; Kopelman, 1985; McKee and Squire, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Freed et al., 1987; Kopelman, 1985; McKee and Squire, 1992.

claim: Standard consolidation theory holds that newly-acquired memories initially depend upon the hippocampus but gradually become hippocampus-independent through consolidation.
source: The 'standard consolidation theory' holds that newly-acquired memories initially depend upon the HPC but that, through a process of 'consolidation', memory traces gradually become HPC-independent and are stored in and retrieved by neocortical structures alone (Hardt and Nadel, 2018; Squire et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hardt and Nadel, 2018 and Squire et al., 2015.

claim: Multiple trace theory proposes that the hippocampus is necessary for vivid episodic recollection irrespective of the age of the memory.
source: In contrast, 'multiple trace theory' proposes that the HPC is necessary for vivid episodic recollection irrespective of the age of the memory (Moscovitch et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moscovitch et al., 2005.

claim: Hippocampal amnesia is very rare.
source: A central problem for addressing these debates with neuropsychology and, more specifically, for determining the relevance of wider brain network abnormalities, is that HPC amnesia is very rare.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of hippocampal amnesia, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most studies of hippocampal amnesia rely upon just a handful of amnesic cases.
source: Consequently, most studies rely upon just a handful of amnesic cases and are thus susceptible to confounds such as impairment severity, measurement noise and individual differences (Lambon Ralph et al., 2011; Lambon Ralph et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lambon Ralph et al., 2011 and Lambon Ralph et al., 2002.

claim: Studies with small numbers of amnesic cases are susceptible to confounds such as impairment severity, measurement noise and individual differences.
source: Consequently, most studies rely upon just a handful of amnesic cases and are thus susceptible to confounds such as impairment severity, measurement noise and individual differences (Lambon Ralph et al., 2011; Lambon Ralph et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lambon Ralph et al., 2011 and Lambon Ralph et al., 2002.

claim: Larger cohort studies would partially overcome confounds related to impairment severity, measurement noise and individual differences.
source: Larger cohort studies would partially overcome these confounds and capitalize on case heterogeneity to map behavior to brain structure and function.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of larger sample sizes in research.

claim: The study examined a cohort of 38 patients after autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: In order to explore the impact of HPC damage on wider brain networks and determine the impact of these abnormalities upon memory, we studied a uniquely large cohort (n = 38) of patients after autoimmune limbic encephalitis (LE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and sample.

claim: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis classically causes focal hippocampal damage in its acute phase.
source: In its acute phase, this highly consistent clinical syndrome classically causes focal HPC damage, seen on MRI as high T2 signal (Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014.

claim: Focal hippocampal damage in autoimmune limbic encephalitis is seen on MRI as high T2 signal.
source: In its acute phase, this highly consistent clinical syndrome classically causes focal HPC damage, seen on MRI as high T2 signal (Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014.

claim: Most autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients respond well to early immunosuppressive therapy.
source: Although most patients respond well to early immunosuppressive therapy (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2018), some subsequently develop HPC atrophy and persistent cognitive impairment, the most prominent aspect of which is anterograde amnesia (Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2018.

claim: Some autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients subsequently develop hippocampal atrophy and persistent cognitive impairment.
source: Although most patients respond well to early immunosuppressive therapy (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2018), some subsequently develop HPC atrophy and persistent cognitive impairment, the most prominent aspect of which is anterograde amnesia (Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014.

claim: The most prominent aspect of persistent cognitive impairment in autoimmune limbic encephalitis is anterograde amnesia.
source: Although most patients respond well to early immunosuppressive therapy (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2018), some subsequently develop HPC atrophy and persistent cognitive impairment, the most prominent aspect of which is anterograde amnesia (Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019; Malter et al., 2014.

claim: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients are often included in studies of hippocampal amnesia.
source: Autoimmune LE patients are often included in studies of HPC amnesia (Hassabis et al., 2007; Henson et al., 2017; Henson et al., 2016; Maguire et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hassabis et al., 2007; Henson et al., 2017; Henson et al., 2016; Maguire et al., 2006.

claim: Post-mortem studies demonstrate focal hippocampal damage in autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: Post-mortem studies demonstrate focal HPC damage (Khan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2007), contrasting with the wider damage typically found following other encephalitides [e.g. herpes simplex encephalitis (Damasio and Van Hoesen, 1985; Gitelman et al., 2001)] or global ischemia/anoxia (Huang and Castillo, 2008), conditions that have also been used as models of human HPC function (for discussion, see Squire and Zola, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khan et al., 2009 and Park et al., 2007.

claim: Herpes simplex encephalitis typically results in wider damage than autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: Post-mortem studies demonstrate focal HPC damage (Khan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2007), contrasting with the wider damage typically found following other encephalitides [e.g. herpes simplex encephalitis (Damasio and Van Hoesen, 1985; Gitelman et al., 2001)] or global ischemia/anoxia (Huang and Castillo, 2008), conditions that have also been used as models of human HPC function (for discussion, see Squire and Zola, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Damasio and Van Hoesen, 1985 and Gitelman et al., 2001.

claim: Global ischemia/anoxia typically results in wider damage than autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: Post-mortem studies demonstrate focal HPC damage (Khan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2007), contrasting with the wider damage typically found following other encephalitides [e.g. herpes simplex encephalitis (Damasio and Van Hoesen, 1985; Gitelman et al., 2001)] or global ischemia/anoxia (Huang and Castillo, 2008), conditions that have also been used as models of human HPC function (for discussion, see Squire and Zola, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huang and Castillo, 2008.

claim: Animal models of autoimmune limbic encephalitis have shown focal limbic involvement (hippocampus, amygdala).
source: Animal models have also shown focal limbic involvement (HPC, amygdala) (Tröscher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tröscher et al., 2017.

claim: Patients and healthy controls were assessed with a thorough battery of neuropsychological tests of episodic memory and other cognitive functions.
source: Patients (n = 38) and healthy controls (n = 41) were assessed with a thorough battery of neuropsychological tests of episodic memory (for verbal and visual material) and other cognitive functions, in order to identify the tasks in which patients showed impaired performance.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study used manual volumetry of medial temporal lobe regions to identify regions of gray matter volume reduction in patients.
source: Using manual volumetry of MTL regions, as well as whole-brain, voxel-based investigations of structural MRI, we identified regions of gray matter (GM) volume reduction in patients as compared with healthy controls.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study used whole-brain, voxel-based investigations of structural MRI to identify regions of gray matter volume reduction in patients.
source: Using manual volumetry of MTL regions, as well as whole-brain, voxel-based investigations of structural MRI, we identified regions of gray matter (GM) volume reduction in patients as compared with healthy controls.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study used resting-state fMRI to identify resting-state functional abnormalities in patients.
source: Using resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI), we also identified resting-state functional abnormalities in patients with respect to both segregation and integration, that is in terms of hemodynamic activity in local regions (resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations; rsALFF) and functional connectivity between regions (resting-state functional connectivity; rsFC).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study predicted that hippocampal damage would be accompanied by remote abnormalities in hubs of the extended hippocampal system.
source: We predicted that: i) HPC damage (documented to occur focally in autoimmune LE) would be accompanied by remote abnormalities in hubs of the extended HPC system, including the HPC-diencephalic-cingulate network (Aggleton, 2014; Bubb et al., 2017);
evidence: This is a statement of the study's hypothesis.

claim: The study predicted that variation in the extent of network-wide abnormalities across patients would explain variability in memory impairment over and above hippocampal atrophy.
source: ii) variation in the extent of these network-wide abnormalities across patients would explain variability in memory impairment over and above HPC atrophy;
evidence: This is a statement of the study's hypothesis.

claim: The study predicted that relationships between hippocampal atrophy and memory impairment would be mediated by network disruption.
source: iii) Moreover, on our assumption that HPC damage leads to broader network disruption, we predicted that relationships between HPC atrophy and memory impairment would be mediated by this network disruption.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's hypothesis.

claim: The study predicted that taking network abnormalities into account would enable identification of which aspects of memory impairment are a direct function of hippocampal atrophy.
source: iv) taking these abnormalities into account would enable us to identify which particular aspects of memory impairment are a direct function of HPC atrophy.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's hypothesis.

claim: Patients did not differ from healthy controls in premorbid intelligence, semantic memory and language, visuomotor and executive function.
source: Patients did not differ from healthy controls (n = 41; matched for age and M:F ratio) in premorbid intelligence, semantic memory and language, visuomotor and executive function.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients' cognitive profile was characterized by highly focal episodic memory impairment.
source: Their cognitive profile was characterized by highly focal episodic memory impairment.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients were impaired in both recall and recognition of both verbal and visual material.
source: Patients were impaired in both recall and recognition of both verbal and visual material (including scenes), and showed pronounced forgetting of visual material – verbal forgetting was marginally impaired.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed pronounced forgetting of visual material.
source: Patients were impaired in both recall and recognition of both verbal and visual material (including scenes), and showed pronounced forgetting of visual material – verbal forgetting was marginally impaired.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed marginally impaired verbal forgetting.
source: Patients were impaired in both recall and recognition of both verbal and visual material (including scenes), and showed pronounced forgetting of visual material – verbal forgetting was marginally impaired.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed preserved face recognition memory.
source: A clear exception was patients' preserved face recognition memory.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed impaired remote autobiographical memory for both childhood and early adulthood epochs.
source: They also showed impaired remote autobiographical memory for both childhood and early adulthood epochs, but preserved remote personal semantic memory.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed preserved remote personal semantic memory.
source: They also showed impaired remote autobiographical memory for both childhood and early adulthood epochs, but preserved remote personal semantic memory.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Patients showed higher scores on the depression sub-scale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale than controls.
source: Although they showed higher scores on the depression sub-scale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) (Zigmond and Snaith, 1983), the median score was well below the clinical cut-off, and none of the patients scored within the severe range (mild range: three patients; moderate range: four patients; non-case range: rest of patients and all controls) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: The median depression score in patients was well below the clinical cut-off.
source: Although they showed higher scores on the depression sub-scale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) (Zigmond and Snaith, 1983), the median score was well below the clinical cut-off, and none of the patients scored within the severe range (mild range: three patients; moderate range: four patients; non-case range: rest of patients and all controls) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: None of the patients scored within the severe range on the depression sub-scale.
source: Although they showed higher scores on the depression sub-scale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) (Zigmond and Snaith, 1983), the median score was well below the clinical cut-off, and none of the patients scored within the severe range (mild range: three patients; moderate range: four patients; non-case range: rest of patients and all controls) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on neuropsychological assessment data.

claim: Volumetric analysis revealed pronounced bilateral hippocampal atrophy in patients.
source: Consistent with the neuroradiological reports on patients' acute clinical T2-weighted MRI scans (Table 2) and the fact that acute HPC T2 hyperintensity and oedema are followed by post-acute HPC atrophy in autoimmune LE (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019), volumetric analysis of patients' post-acute MRIs revealed pronounced bilateral HPC atrophy (left HPC: F = 46.02, p-corr <0.0005; right HPC: F = 63.38, p-corr <0.0005).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on volumetric analysis of MRI data.

claim: Acute hippocampal T2 hyperintensity and oedema are followed by post-acute hippocampal atrophy in autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: Consistent with the neuroradiological reports on patients' acute clinical T2-weighted MRI scans (Table 2) and the fact that acute HPC T2 hyperintensity and oedema are followed by post-acute HPC atrophy in autoimmune LE (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019), volumetric analysis of patients' post-acute MRIs revealed pronounced bilateral HPC atrophy (left HPC: F = 46.02, p-corr <0.0005; right HPC: F = 63.38, p-corr <0.0005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Loane et al., 2019.

claim: Patients showed right entorhinal cortical volume reduction.
source: We also observed right entorhinal (F = 10.76, p-corr = 0.0308) and left thalamic volume reduction (F = 15.41, p-corr = 0.0003; Table 3).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on volumetric analysis of MRI data.

claim: Patients showed left thalamic volume reduction.
source: We also observed right entorhinal (F = 10.76, p-corr = 0.0308) and left thalamic volume reduction (F = 15.41, p-corr = 0.0003; Table 3).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on volumetric analysis of MRI data.

claim: A whole-brain VBM contrast disclosed reduced gray matter volume in patients' left and right hippocampus.
source: Strongly consistent with the volumetric findings above, a whole-brain VBM contrast disclosed reduced GM volume in patients' left and right HPC, as well as in the anterior/mediodorsal, and right dorsolateral regions of the thalamus (Figure 2a; Table 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on voxel-based morphometry analysis. Figure 2a shows the VBM results.

claim: A whole-brain VBM contrast disclosed reduced gray matter volume in the anterior/mediodorsal and right dorsolateral regions of the thalamus.
source: Strongly consistent with the volumetric findings above, a whole-brain VBM contrast disclosed reduced GM volume in patients' left and right HPC, as well as in the anterior/mediodorsal, and right dorsolateral regions of the thalamus (Figure 2a; Table 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on voxel-based morphometry analysis. Figure 2a shows the VBM results.

claim: Patients showed reduced resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the posterior cingulate cortex.
source: As compared with healthy controls, patients showed reduced rsALFF in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the precuneus (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on resting-state fMRI analysis. Figure 2b shows the reduced rsALFF in the PCC.

claim: Patients showed reduced resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the precuneus.
source: As compared with healthy controls, patients showed reduced rsALFF in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the precuneus (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on resting-state fMRI analysis. Figure 2c shows the reduced rsALFF in the precuneus.

claim: The effect of average hippocampal volume reduction on the resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations of the posterior cingulate cortex was fully mediated by average thalamic volume reduction.
source: Consistent with the reciprocal connectivity of thalamic nuclei with both the HPC and the cingulate cortex (Aggleton, 2014; Aggleton et al., 2010; Bubb et al., 2017) and our hypothesis that HPC atrophy is followed by structural and functional abnormalities in interconnected areas within the HPC-diencephalic-cingulate networks, we observed that the effect of average HPC volume reduction on the rsALFF of the PCC was fully mediated by average thalamic volume reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: Thalamic nuclei have reciprocal connectivity with both the hippocampus and the cingulate cortex.
source: Consistent with the reciprocal connectivity of thalamic nuclei with both the HPC and the cingulate cortex (Aggleton, 2014; Aggleton et al., 2010; Bubb et al., 2017) and our hypothesis that HPC atrophy is followed by structural and functional abnormalities in interconnected areas within the HPC-diencephalic-cingulate networks, we observed that the effect of average HPC volume reduction on the rsALFF of the PCC was fully mediated by average thalamic volume reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplements 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aggleton, 2014; Aggleton et al., 2010; Bubb et al., 2017.

claim: A connectome-MVPA analysis showed group differences in the whole-brain resting-state functional connectivity of a right hippocampal cluster.
source: This analysis showed group differences in the whole-brain rsFC of a right HPC cluster (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on connectome-MVPA analysis. Figure 2d shows the right hippocampal cluster.

claim: The right hippocampus showed reduced resting-state functional connectivity with the medial prefrontal cortex in patients.
source: The spatially unsmoothed timeseries data were extracted from participants' manually delineated right HPC in native space, ensuring that rsFC differences were not an artefact of insufficient co-registration of the atrophic HPC. This seed region showed reduced rsFC with clusters in the medial prefrontal and posteromedial (PCC, retrosplenial, and precuneus) cortices, and the left HPC (Figure 2e–g).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on seed-to-voxel resting-state functional connectivity analysis. Figure 2e shows the reduced rsFC with the medial prefrontal cortex.

claim: The right hippocampus showed reduced resting-state functional connectivity with the posteromedial cortex (posterior cingulate, retrosplenial, and precuneus) in patients.
source: The spatially unsmoothed timeseries data were extracted from participants' manually delineated right HPC in native space, ensuring that rsFC differences were not an artefact of insufficient co-registration of the atrophic HPC. This seed region showed reduced rsFC with clusters in the medial prefrontal and posteromedial (PCC, retrosplenial, and precuneus) cortices, and the left HPC (Figure 2e–g).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on seed-to-voxel resting-state functional connectivity analysis. Figure 2f shows the reduced rsFC with the posteromedial cortex.

claim: The right hippocampus showed reduced resting-state functional connectivity with the left hippocampus in patients.
source: The spatially unsmoothed timeseries data were extracted from participants' manually delineated right HPC in native space, ensuring that rsFC differences were not an artefact of insufficient co-registration of the atrophic HPC. This seed region showed reduced rsFC with clusters in the medial prefrontal and posteromedial (PCC, retrosplenial, and precuneus) cortices, and the left HPC (Figure 2e–g).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on seed-to-voxel resting-state functional connectivity analysis. Figure 2g shows the reduced rsFC with the left hippocampus.

claim: Patients' reduced inter-hippocampal resting-state functional connectivity negatively correlated with the delay between the onset of their symptoms and the time they underwent research MRI.
source: Patients' reduced inter-HPC rsFC (of all 13 structural and functional abnormalities) negatively correlated, across patients, with the delay between the onset of their symptoms and the time they underwent our research MRI (Supplementary Table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: Anterograde retrieval scores correlated across patients with their reduced resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the posterior cingulate cortex.
source: Three correlations survived correction for multiple tests: i) Anterograde retrieval scores correlated across patients with their reduced rsALFF in the PCC (r = 0.551; p-corr = 0.024);
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: Anterograde retention (forgetting) scores correlated with patients' reduced right hippocampal volume.
source: ii) Anterograde retention (i.e. 'forgetting') scores correlated with patients' reduced right HPC volume (VBM cluster; rho = 0.556, p-corr = 0.024; manually delineated right HPC volume: rho = 0.508, p-corr = 0.079);
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: Remote autobiographical memory scores correlated with patients' reduced volume in the left thalamus.
source: iii) Remote autobiographical memory scores correlated with patients' reduced volume in the left thalamus (r = 0.558; p-corr = 0.041; rest of ps, p-corr ≥0.105; Supplementary Table 3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: Verbal recognition scores correlated with patients' reduced inter-hippocampal resting-state functional connectivity.
source: Verbal recognition scores correlated with patients' reduced inter-HPC rsFC (r = 0.498, p-corr = 0.039; rest of ps, p-corr ≥0.18; Figure 3b; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis. Figure 3b shows the correlation.

claim: The volume expressed by the left hippocampal VBM cluster correlated with verbal recognition scores at uncorrected levels.
source: Out of the HPC volumes, only the volume expressed by the left HPC VBM cluster correlated with verbal recognition scores at uncorrected levels (r = 0.360, p-unc = 0.029; Figure 3a; rest of rs, 0.281 ≥ r ≥ 0.276; rest of ps, 0.098 ≥ p unc ≥ 0.092).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis. Figure 3a shows the correlation.

claim: Inter-hippocampal resting-state functional connectivity was the only predictor of patients' verbal recognition performance in multiple step-wise linear regressions.
source: We thus entered mean inter-HPC rsFC and one of those four HPC volume measures as independent variables in four separate multiple step-wise linear regressions, with verbal recognition scores as the dependent variable. In all four analyses, the regression terminated in a single step, with inter-HPC rsFC as the only predictor of patients' performance (R2 = 0.25; β(z) = 0.50; F = 10.53, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on multiple step-wise linear regression analysis.

claim: Visual recognition scores correlated with patients' reduced resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the posterior cingulate cortex.
source: Visual recognition scores correlated with patients' reduced rsALFF in the PCC (r = 0.543, p-corr = 0.014), and only marginally with the volume of the left HPC VBM cluster (r = 0.449, p-corr = 0.072; rest of ps, p-corr ≥0.110).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: The effects of left hippocampal volume reduction on visual recognition scores were fully mediated by the reduction in posterior cingulate cortex resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.
source: Indeed, the effects of left HPC volume reduction on visual recognition scores were fully mediated by the reduction in PCC rsALFF (direct effect: β = 0.24, p=0.183; indirect effect: β = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.41) (Figure 4; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 4 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: Verbal recall memory composite scores correlated across patients with their reduced posterior cingulate cortex resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.
source: Verbal recall memory composite scores correlated across patients with their reduced PCC rsALFF (r = 0.582, p-corr = 0.004) and with the volume of the left HPC VBM cluster (r = 0.495, p-corr = 0.024; rest of ps, p-corr ≥0.290).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: Verbal recall memory composite scores correlated with the volume of the left hippocampal VBM cluster.
source: Verbal recall memory composite scores correlated across patients with their reduced PCC rsALFF (r = 0.582, p-corr = 0.004) and with the volume of the left HPC VBM cluster (r = 0.495, p-corr = 0.024; rest of ps, p-corr ≥0.290).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: The effects of hippocampal atrophy on verbal recall were fully mediated by the reduction in posterior cingulate cortex resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the effects of HPC atrophy on verbal recall were fully mediated by the reduction in PCC rsALFF (direct effect: β = 0.16, p=0.124; indirect effect: β = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.29; Figure 5; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 5 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: The effects of hippocampal atrophy on visual recall were fully mediated by the reduction in posterior cingulate cortex resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.
source: The effects of HPC atrophy on visual recall were fully mediated by the reduction in PCC rsALFF (direct effect: β = 0.23, p=0.272; indirect effect: β = 0.19, 95% CI:0.01,0.46) (Figure 6; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 6 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: Anterograde retention (visual forgetting) scores correlated only with volume reduction in the right hippocampal VBM cluster.
source: Anterograde retention (visual forgetting) scores correlated only with volume reduction in the right HPC VBM cluster (rho = 0.556, p-corr = 0.008) and in the manually delineated right HPC (rho = 0.508, p-corr = 0.026; an alternative analysis, comparing patients that scored at ceiling with the rest of the patient group, is reported in Supplementary Table 6 in Supplementary file 1, disclosing the same relationships).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on correlation analysis.

claim: The effect of right hippocampal volume reduction on visual forgetting scores remained unmediated by the correlative reduction in posterior cingulate cortex resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.
source: The strong relationship of visual forgetting scores with right HPC volumes across patients was further demonstrated by a mediation analysis, whereby the effect of right HPC volume reduction on visual forgetting scores remained unmediated by the correlative reduction in PCC rsALFF across patients (direct effect: β = 0.43, p=0.036; indirect effect: β = 0.10, 95% CI: −0.11,0.32; Figure 7; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 7 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: The effects of left hippocampal atrophy on remote autobiographical memory were fully mediated by volume reduction in the left thalamus.
source: Moreover, the effects of left HPC atrophy on remote autobiographical memory were fully mediated by volume reduction in the left thalamus (direct effect: β = 0.94, p=0.165; indirect effect: β = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.20, 1.89; Figure 8; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results, based on mediation analysis. Figure 8 shows the mediation analysis results.

claim: Associations of hippocampal volume with recall, recognition, and remote memory were fully mediated by wider network abnormalities.
source: Associations of hippocampal volume with recall, recognition, and remote memory were fully mediated by wider network abnormalities, and were only direct in forgetting.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Associations of hippocampal volume with forgetting were direct and not mediated by wider network abnormalities.
source: Associations of hippocampal volume with recall, recognition, and remote memory were fully mediated by wider network abnormalities, and were only direct in forgetting.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Patients showed impaired recall, recognition and maintenance of new information.
source: These patients showed impaired recall, recognition and maintenance of new information, and remote autobiographical amnesia.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Patients showed remote autobiographical amnesia.
source: These patients showed impaired recall, recognition and maintenance of new information, and remote autobiographical amnesia.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Besides hippocampal atrophy, patients showed correlatively reduced thalamic and entorhinal cortical volume.
source: Besides hippocampal atrophy, we observed correlatively reduced thalamic and entorhinal cortical volume, resting-state inter-hippocampal connectivity and activity in posteromedial cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Patients showed reduced resting-state inter-hippocampal connectivity.
source: Besides hippocampal atrophy, we observed correlatively reduced thalamic and entorhinal cortical volume, resting-state inter-hippocampal connectivity and activity in posteromedial cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Patients showed reduced activity in posteromedial cortex.
source: Besides hippocampal atrophy, we observed correlatively reduced thalamic and entorhinal cortical volume, resting-state inter-hippocampal connectivity and activity in posteromedial cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's results.

claim: Network abnormalities may explain the variability across studies of amnesia.
source: Network abnormalities may explain the variability across studies of amnesia and speak to debates in memory neuroscience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: The study examined 38 patients after autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: We identified 38 patients (26M:12F; age at research MRI: M = 63.06; IQR = 16.16 years; Table 2) who i) had undergone neuropsychological assessment during the acute phase of the illness at the Russell Cairns Unit, Oxford (2013–2018);
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: 34 out of 38 patients met the criteria for a diagnosis of 'definite limbic encephalitis'.
source: 34/38 patients met the criteria for a diagnosis of 'definite LE'.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: In the majority of patients (28/38), an autoantibody known to be associated with limbic encephalitis had been identified.
source: In the majority of patients (28/38), an autoantibody known to be associated with LE had been identified, but 10/38 had the typical clinical profile of LE with no identified antibody.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: 10 out of 38 patients had the typical clinical profile of limbic encephalitis with no identified antibody.
source: In the majority of patients (28/38), an autoantibody known to be associated with LE had been identified, but 10/38 had the typical clinical profile of LE with no identified antibody.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Cases of limbic encephalitis with no identified antibody are well-recognised.
source: Such cases are well-recognised (Graus et al., 2018) and are likely here due to antibodies not detectable in routine clinical practice at the time of screening.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Graus et al., 2018.

claim: 31 out of 38 patients had been treated with immunotherapy in the acute phase of the illness.
source: 31/38 patients had been treated with immunotherapy (e.g. intravenous and/or oral prednisolone, plasma exchange) in the acute phase of the illness.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: 34 out of 38 patients showed abnormal signal, volume (swelling or atrophy) and/or (facilitated) diffusion in the hippocampus on acute clinical MRI.
source: 34/38 patients showed abnormal signal, volume (swelling or atrophy) and/or (facilitated) diffusion in the HPC.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: High signal in the amygdala was noted in 6 out of 38 patients on acute clinical MRI.
source: High signal in the amygdala was noted in 6/38 patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: No acute abnormalities were detected in 4 out of 38 patients who nonetheless had clinical features characteristic of autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
source: No acute abnormalities were detected in 4/38 patients who nonetheless had clinical features characteristic of autoimmune LE.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: Only one patient showed extra-medial temporal lobe abnormalities (bright caudate) on acute clinical MRI.
source: Only one patient showed extra-MTL abnormalities (bright caudate), and four patients had mild microangiopathic changes, which are commonly found with aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: Four patients had mild microangiopathic changes on acute clinical MRI, which are commonly found with aging.
source: Only one patient showed extra-MTL abnormalities (bright caudate), and four patients had mild microangiopathic changes, which are commonly found with aging.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: The study used a composite score for anterograde retrieval comprising scores on tests of verbal recall, verbal recognition, visual recall, and visual recognition.
source: For the purposes of data reduction, minimization of measurement error, maximization of generalizability of our findings, and simplification of correlational analyses, we used i) an anterograde memory composite score for visual recall (D and P Shapes, ROCFT Immediate and Delayed Recall), verbal recall (WMS-III Logical Memory I,II, Word List I,II, D and P People), visual recognition (RMT Scenes, D and P Doors), and verbal recognition memory (RMT Words, D and P Names, WMS-III Word List Recognition), reflecting 'anterograde retrieval', by averaging the age-scaled, standardized scores of each patient across the tests of anterograde memory in which patients showed group-level impairment;
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study used a remote autobiographical memory score calculated by summing the scores on autobiographical memories for childhood and early adulthood epochs from the Autobiographical Memory Interview.
source: ii) a remote autobiographical memory score, by summing patients' AMI scores for autobiographical memories in childhood and early adulthood;
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The study used the Doors and People scores for verbal and/or visual forgetting.
source: iii) the D and P scores for verbal and/or visual forgetting - unlike other tests of immediate and delayed recall memory that involve no mechanism for equating participants on immediate recall, the D and P quantifies forgetting on the basis of participants' performance in the last trial of immediate recall relative to their performance in delayed recall.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methods.

claim: The Doors and People test quantifies forgetting on the basis of participants' performance in the last trial of immediate recall relative to their performance in delayed recall.
source: iii) the D and P scores for verbal and/or visual forgetting - unlike other tests of immediate and delayed recall memory that involve no mechanism for equating participants on immediate recall, the D and P quantifies forgetting on the basis of participants' performance in the last trial of immediate recall relative to their performance in delayed recall.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Doors and People test.

claim: Acute inflammatory changes appeared confined to the hippocampus in the vast majority of patients.
source: Nevertheless, acute inflammatory changes appeared confined to the HPC in the vast majority of our patients, while no such changes were found in the thalamus.
evidence: This is a statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: No acute inflammatory changes were found in the thalamus.
source: Nevertheless, acute inflammatory changes appeared confined to the HPC in the vast majority of our patients, while no such changes were found in the thalamus.
evidence: This is a statement about the acute clinical MRI findings.

claim: Clinical T2-weighted MRIs in other autoimmune limbic encephalitis cohorts have demonstrated focal, acute hippocampal pathology.
source: Moreover, clinical T2-weighted MRIs in other autoimmune LE cohorts (Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Malter et al., 2014), and the results of post-mortem studies have also demonstrated focal, acute HPC pathology in autoimmune LE patients (Khan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2007) and animal models (Tröscher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Finke et al., 2017; Kotsenas et al., 2014; Malter et al., 2014.

claim: Extra-hippocampal structures within the extended hippocampal system (thalamus, posterior cingulate cortex) are affected as a secondary consequence of hippocampal damage.
source: Our interpretation of these data is, therefore, that extra-HPC structures within the extended HPC system (thalamus, PCC) are affected as a secondary consequence of HPC damage, rather than due to the primary pathology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Extra-hippocampal damage is equally if not more likely in other conditions associated with hippocampal amnesia, such as cases of ischemia/anoxia.
source: We also note that extra-HPC damage is equally if not more likely in other conditions associated with HPC amnesia, such as cases of ischemia/anoxia (Huang and Castillo, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huang and Castillo, 2008.

claim: A single case study of amnesia due to ischemia/anoxia which came to post mortem demonstrated focal neuronal loss in the CA1 region of the hippocampus on histopathology.
source: It should, however, be acknowledged that a single case study of amnesia due to ischemia/anoxia which came to post mortem demonstrated focal neuronal loss in the CA1 region of the HPC on histopathology (Zola-Morgan et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zola-Morgan et al., 1986.

claim: Patients showed functional abnormalities in the posteromedial cortex.
source: Patients also showed functional abnormalities in the posteromedial cortex, and the relationship between HPC atrophy and PCC rsALFF was fully mediated by the correlative volume reduction in the thalamic regions.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results.

claim: Functional abnormalities have been observed in posteromedial cortical regions in both hippocampal and diencephalic amnesias in humans.
source: This is consistent with the functional abnormalities previously observed in posteromedial cortical regions in both HPC and diencephalic amnesias in humans (Aggleton, 2014; Reed et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aggleton, 2014 and Reed et al., 1999.

claim: In healthy individuals, the spontaneous activity of the hippocampus is coupled with that of the contralateral hippocampus at rest.
source: In healthy individuals, the spontaneous activity of the HPC is coupled with that of the contralateral HPC at rest and these regions form part of the default-mode network.
evidence: This is a statement about brain function in healthy individuals, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: The hippocampus forms part of the default-mode network.
source: In healthy individuals, the spontaneous activity of the HPC is coupled with that of the contralateral HPC at rest and these regions form part of the default-mode network. This is also the case for the medial prefrontal and posteromedial cortical regions which showed reduced rsFC with the HPC (Buckner et al., 2008; Greicius et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buckner et al., 2008 and Greicius et al., 2004.

claim: The medial prefrontal and posteromedial cortical regions form part of the default-mode network.
source: In healthy individuals, the spontaneous activity of the HPC is coupled with that of the contralateral HPC at rest and these regions form part of the default-mode network. This is also the case for the medial prefrontal and posteromedial cortical regions which showed reduced rsFC with the HPC (Buckner et al., 2008; Greicius et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buckner et al., 2008 and Greicius et al., 2004.

claim: The decrease in inter-hippocampal resting-state functional connectivity across patients as a function of delay since symptom onset is consistent with the idea that network-wide abnormalities follow focal hippocampal damage.
source: The decrease in inter-HPC rsFC across patients as a function of delay since symptom onset is consistent with the idea that these network-wide abnormalities follow focal HPC damage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Recognition of unfamiliar faces may be holistically processed and difficult to label verbally.
source: This would be predicted by some material-specific accounts of recognition memory (Bird and Burgess, 2008) and is consistent with the view that recognition of unfamiliar faces is exceptional in several regards – according to some approaches, faces may be holistically processed and difficult to label verbally, and adequate performance levels may be attained in the absence of capacities to associate faces with a study list (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2014.

claim: Adequate performance levels in face recognition may be attained in the absence of capacities to associate faces with a study list.
source: This would be predicted by some material-specific accounts of recognition memory (Bird and Burgess, 2008) and is consistent with the view that recognition of unfamiliar faces is exceptional in several regards – according to some approaches, faces may be holistically processed and difficult to label verbally, and adequate performance levels may be attained in the absence of capacities to associate faces with a study list (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2014.

claim: The posteromedial cortex has a causal role in episodic memory for both visual and verbal material.
source: It furthermore dovetails with the causal role that has been attributed to the posteromedial cortex in episodic memory for both visual (Bonnì et al., 2015) and verbal (Koch et al., 2018) material, and aligns with evidence from neurodegenerative diseases that it is posteromedial cortex rather than HPC function that predicts episodic memory impairment (La Joie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonnì et al., 2015 and Koch et al., 2018.

claim: In neurodegenerative diseases, it is posteromedial cortex rather than hippocampal function that predicts episodic memory impairment.
source: It furthermore dovetails with the causal role that has been attributed to the posteromedial cortex in episodic memory for both visual (Bonnì et al., 2015) and verbal (Koch et al., 2018) material, and aligns with evidence from neurodegenerative diseases that it is posteromedial cortex rather than HPC function that predicts episodic memory impairment (La Joie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to La Joie et al., 2014.

claim: The relationship between inter-hippocampal connectivity and episodic memory has been found in healthy populations.
source: The relationship with inter-HPC rsFC is consistent with that found between inter-HPC connectivity and episodic memory in healthy (Wang et al., 2010) and patient populations (e.g. traumatic axonal injury) (Marquez de la Plata et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The relationship between inter-hippocampal connectivity and episodic memory has been found in patient populations such as traumatic axonal injury.
source: The relationship with inter-HPC rsFC is consistent with that found between inter-HPC connectivity and episodic memory in healthy (Wang et al., 2010) and patient populations (e.g. traumatic axonal injury) (Marquez de la Plata et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marquez de la Plata et al., 2011.

claim: The volumes and hemodynamic activity of hippocampal subfields have been associated with various forms of memory.
source: The volumes and hemodynamic activity of HPC subfields have been associated with various forms of memory (Bonnici et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017; Palombo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonnici et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017; Palombo et al., 2018.

claim: Hippocampal amnesic patients differ in the form and content of their 'mind-wandering' compared with healthy adults.
source: McCormick and colleagues recently showed that HPC amnesic patients differ in the form and content of their 'mind-wandering' compared with healthy adults (McCormick et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McCormick et al., 2018.

claim: Resting-state fMRI measures have repeatedly provided reliable correlates of memory impairment in hippocampal amnesia.
source: Nevertheless, rsfMRI measures (predominantly rsFC) have repeatedly provided reliable correlates of memory impairment in HPC amnesia [e.g. (Heine et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016)].
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heine et al., 2018 and Henson et al., 2016.

claim: Rapid forgetting of visual information in right hippocampal damage was noted quite early.
source: Indeed, rapid forgetting of visual information in right HPC damage was noted quite early (Jones-Gotman, 1986), as was, in general, the nature of forgetting in HPC amnesia (Huppert and Piercy, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jones-Gotman, 1986.

claim: Functional neuroimaging studies in healthy young adults attribute a central role to the hippocampus in constraining the forgetting that occurs by new learning.
source: This has recently been re-emphasized (Sadeh et al., 2014), with functional neuroimaging studies in healthy young adults attributing a central role to the HPC in constraining the forgetting that occurs by new learning (Kuhl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sadeh et al., 2014 and Kuhl et al., 2010.

claim: Pattern completion enables the reinstatement of previously encoded memories from incomplete input.
source: This relationship is consistent with computational models of HPC function that outline pattern completion and pattern separation (O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994) as two core mechanisms that protect against forgetting. Pattern completion enables the reinstatement of previously encoded memories from incomplete input, whereas pattern separation involves the orthogonal coding of memories for overlapping events, which minimizes forgetting by generating non-interfering representations (Kuhl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994 and Kuhl et al., 2010.

claim: Pattern separation involves the orthogonal coding of memories for overlapping events, which minimizes forgetting by generating non-interfering representations.
source: This relationship is consistent with computational models of HPC function that outline pattern completion and pattern separation (O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994) as two core mechanisms that protect against forgetting. Pattern completion enables the reinstatement of previously encoded memories from incomplete input, whereas pattern separation involves the orthogonal coding of memories for overlapping events, which minimizes forgetting by generating non-interfering representations (Kuhl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994 and Kuhl et al., 2010.

claim: The hippocampal role in amnesia may be much less direct than has previously been held, at least with respect to performance on widely used, standardized neuropsychological tests of memory.
source: These findings suggest that the HPC role in amnesia may be much less direct than has previously been held, at least with respect to performance on widely used, standardized neuropsychological tests of memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: The direct relationship of right hippocampal atrophy with visual forgetting highlights the utility of tests of accelerated forgetting in detecting hippocampal pathology in other disorders.
source: Nevertheless, the direct relationship of (right) HPC atrophy with (visual) forgetting highlights the utility of tests of accelerated forgetting in detecting HPC pathology in other disorders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: Recent studies have emphasized a possible role for tests of accelerated forgetting in the early detection of Alzheimer's disease pathology.
source: Recent studies have emphasized a possible role for such tests in the early detection of Alzheimer's disease pathology (Weston et al., 2018; Zimmermann and Butler, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weston et al., 2018 and Zimmermann and Butler, 2018.

claim: Patients showed spared remote personal semantic memory.
source: Patients showed spared remote personal semantic memory, in the face of impaired remote autobiographical memories.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's results.

claim: Research in autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients has focused on anterograde memory.
source: To date, research in autoimmune LE patients has focused on anterograde memory (Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Henson et al., 2016; Malter et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2017), with very little evidence on retrograde amnesia (Chan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Henson et al., 2016; Malter et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2017.

claim: There is very little evidence on retrograde amnesia in autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients.
source: To date, research in autoimmune LE patients has focused on anterograde memory (Butler et al., 2014; Finke et al., 2017; Henson et al., 2016; Malter et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2017), with very little evidence on retrograde amnesia (Chan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2007.

claim: Studies on other amnesic cohorts have found the Autobiographical Memory Interview and the Autobiographical Interview to offer comparable results.
source: Nevertheless, studies on other amnesic cohorts have found the AMI and the Autobiographical Interview to offer comparable results (Rensen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rensen et al., 2017.

claim: The absence of direct effects of hippocampal atrophy on remote memory, in combination with the selective presence of such effects on forgetting rates, is consistent with the idea that hippocampal circuitry acts as a buffer for the temporary maintenance of episodic information.
source: The absence of direct effects of HPC atrophy on remote memory, in combination with the selective presence of such effects on forgetting rates, is instead consistent with the idea that HPC circuitry acts as a buffer for the temporary maintenance of episodic information, with non-HPC structures storing more permanent memory traces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: Non-hippocampal structures store more permanent memory traces.
source: The absence of direct effects of HPC atrophy on remote memory, in combination with the selective presence of such effects on forgetting rates, is instead consistent with the idea that HPC circuitry acts as a buffer for the temporary maintenance of episodic information, with non-HPC structures storing more permanent memory traces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.

claim: Focal thalamic damage has been often associated with retrograde amnesia in single-case or small case-series studies.
source: Focal thalamic damage has been often associated with retrograde amnesia in single-case or small case-series studies (Carlesimo et al., 2011; Stuss et al., 1988), and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei may coordinate the recollection of cortically stored memories (Miller et al., 2001) via thalamic-prefrontal cortical projections (Kopelman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlesimo et al., 2011 and Stuss et al., 1988.

claim: Mediodorsal thalamic nuclei may coordinate the recollection of cortically stored memories via thalamic-prefrontal cortical projections.
source: Focal thalamic damage has been often associated with retrograde amnesia in single-case or small case-series studies (Carlesimo et al., 2011; Stuss et al., 1988), and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei may coordinate the recollection of cortically stored memories (Miller et al., 2001) via thalamic-prefrontal cortical projections (Kopelman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2001 and Kopelman, 2015.

claim: The study's finding that thalamic volume was reduced in the patient group is consistent with the literature on developmental amnesia due to early hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.
source: Finally, our finding that thalamic volume was reduced in our patient group is consistent with the literature on developmental amnesia due to early hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, where HPC damage has been noted along with atrophy in the thalamus and the mammillary bodies [e.g. (Dzieciol et al., 2017)].
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dzieciol et al., 2017.

claim: In developmental amnesia due to early hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, hippocampal damage has been noted along with atrophy in the thalamus and the mammillary bodies.
source: Finally, our finding that thalamic volume was reduced in our patient group is consistent with the literature on developmental amnesia due to early hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, where HPC damage has been noted along with atrophy in the thalamus and the mammillary bodies [e.g. (Dzieciol et al., 2017)].
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dzieciol et al., 2017.

claim: There is evidence for direct forniceal projections from the hippocampus/subiculum to the anterior thalamus in human and non-human primates.
source: A question for future research is therefore whether adult-onset HPC damage is accompanied by atrophy in the mammillary bodies, or whether thalamic atrophy may occur in the absence of changes to the mammillary bodies, given the evidence for direct forniceal projections from the HPC/subiculum to the anterior thalamus in human and non-human primates (Bubb et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bubb et al., 2017.

claim: Abnormalities in the integrity of and connectivity within the extended hippocampal system may occur after focal hippocampal damage.
source: Our study, probably the largest in human HPC amnesia, shows that abnormalities in the integrity of and connectivity within the extended HPC system may occur after focal HPC damage, and that these play a central role in explaining the variability in the anterograde and retrograde amnesia of patients with HPC atrophy.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's conclusions.

claim: Abnormalities in the integrity of and connectivity within the extended hippocampal system play a central role in explaining the variability in the anterograde and retrograde amnesia of patients with hippocampal atrophy.
source: Our study, probably the largest in human HPC amnesia, shows that abnormalities in the integrity of and connectivity within the extended HPC system may occur after focal HPC damage, and that these play a central role in explaining the variability in the anterograde and retrograde amnesia of patients with HPC atrophy.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's conclusions.

claim: The neuropsychological measure most sensitive and specific to hippocampal atrophy was the forgetting of newly learned information.
source: We found that the neuropsychological measure most sensitive and specific to HPC atrophy was the forgetting of newly learned information.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's conclusions.

claim: Understanding the impact of network-wide changes following hippocampal damage will be key to resolving long-standing controversies in the literature on human amnesia.
source: Understanding the impact of network-wide changes following HPC damage will be key to resolving long-standing controversies in the literature on human amnesia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results.
